## What you build today

A potted PCB, a lubricated and sealed gearbox, and a robot that survives a
static immersion test.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Silicone cure time gates this module

The PCB potting takes **12--24 hours** to cure because of the depth. Plan the
module so potting happens first and soldering happens after the cure, or
across two sittings.
:::

## Before you arrive

| | |
|---|---|
| **Parts** | Waterproofing box, Kapton tape, silicone sealant, USB-C cable, CorrosionX, white lithium grease |
| **Tools** | Needle, soldering iron |
| **Read** | This whole page before starting --- the ordering matters |

## PCB waterproofing

First ensure that the assembled PCB fits within the box before anything else.

1. Tape the bottom side of the box with Kapton.
2. Fill the bottom of the box with silicone sealant until it reaches the USB
   port hole.
3. *Carefully* slide the PCB assembly in, with the Seeeduino facing the bottom
   of the box.
4. **Very important!** Insert a USB-C cable into the port. This keeps the
   sealant from flowing into the port, and the cable is a convenient point to
   hold the assembly by.
5. Add sealant along the three free edges to fill any gaps, until the sealant
   reaches the level of the top side of the PCB. **The PCB components and
   contacts should be left exposed.**
6. Let the silicone cure --- because of the depth this takes about 12--24 h.
7. Solder the wires and contacts.
8. Solder the voltage regulator.
9. Seal the top side of the PCB. The best method here is unclear. Tested
   solutions:
   - Nail polish
   - Silicone sealant
   - [422C silicone conformal coating](https://mgchemicals.com/products/conformal-coatings/silicone-conformal-coatings/conformal-coating-waterproof/)
     ([datasheet](https://mgchemicals.com/downloads/tds/tds-422c-l.pdf))

### If you are on a v2.0 board

The method changes slightly. See [PCB revisions](/reference/pcb.qmd#v2-waterproofing)
for the v2.0 procedure, including the SD-card trap-door recovery and antenna
potting.

## Gearbox

By default the gearbox on the FAAV4 robot is **not waterproof at all**, and it
is normal for it to end up completely filled with water once submerged. Over
years of use the gearbox proved largely immune to corrosion --- after more than
a year of repeated use in water, including in Lake Geneva, one was opened and
showed no sign of corrosion.

That is not the whole story, and the exception is the reason for this step:

![Gearbox and sun gear after a few dives with motor oil lubrication](/Fig/gearbox_rust1.jpg){#fig-rust}

Severe corrosion appeared on a newer robot after only 3--4 uses in water. The
cause is believed to be improper lubrication after cleaning, combined with the
absence of the shaft bearing, which let more water in through the front. Motor
oil had been used as a substitute lubricant; its low viscosity is believed to
have washed it away quickly, leaving the gears dry. Full investigation in
[Design notes](/reference/design-notes.qmd#gearbox-corrosion).

::: {.callout-warning}
## Use the right lubricant

A mix of **CorrosionX and white lithium grease**. Do not substitute motor oil.
Several dives have since been performed with the same gearbox that previously
corroded, and it now runs smoothly.
:::

Parts that rust: **sun gear, planet gears, ring gear, planet shafts.**
Parts that do not: screws, motor shaft, washers, body, circlip.
